requirement:
The reviewer MUST assess the named subject using its text, referenced requirements,
and terminology definitions. For a requirement, the reviewer MUST assess whether
the cited code implements every stated obligation and whether its tests cover the
interesting cases in the design space, including relevant boundaries and failure
cases. When there are no tests, the reviewer MUST assess whether the logic is
simple enough to need no test or a test is impractical to author, and explain that
judgment in the rationale.

For an example, the reviewer MUST assess whether tests exist whose setup and
assertions cover its scenario and expected outcomes. The rationale MUST identify
the relevant sources and explain the implementation and testing judgments for a
requirement, or the test coverage for an example. Referenced requirements provide
context; they MUST NOT become additional subjects to assess in full.
rationale:
**What the requirement asks.** `requirements.ci.review_criteria` governs how the reviewer, which is the authoring model, assesses a subject. For a requirement, it must check that the code implements every obligation and that tests cover the design space, or justify the absence of tests. For an example, it must check that tests cover the scenario and expected outcomes. The rationale must name the sources. Referenced requirements are context only.

**Implementation.**
- The only way the harness can enforce this is through the prompt it gives the reviewer. `fn initial_prompt` in `src/authoring/mod.rs` (about lines 323–355) is annotated `{impl}` for `requirements.ci.review_criteria`. It builds the prompt with `include_str!("../../md/requirements/authoring.md")`, which is the approved template.
- The template text at `md/requirements/authoring.md` lines ~219–245 contains the review guidance:
  - Assess only the named subject, using cited requirements and definitions as context.
  - For a requirement, check that the cited code implements it and that tests cover the interesting design points.
  - If there are no tests, judge whether simplicity or impracticality justifies that, and explain.
  - For an example, check that test setup and assertions cover the scenario and expected outcomes.
  - A true judgment needs a `{test}` reference.
  - The true, FIXME and false outcomes are defined.
  - The rationale must give source locations.
- This guidance covers each obligation in the requirement. The "no test" justification applies to requirements only, matching the example-specific rule in `requirements.examples.evidence`. The template is the single source of truth and is not duplicated in code, so the implementation cannot drift from the documented text.
- The mandatory inputs also give the reviewer the requirement text, referenced definitions and cited code and tests. The bundled skill (`assets/skills/habeas-requirements/SKILL.md` line 20) and `md/reference.md` lines 41–49 also describe these criteria.

**Tests.**
- `ollama_cli_delivers_sources_records_fixme_and_keeps_usage_content_free` (`tests/authoring_cli.rs`, about line 239) carries `{test}` for this requirement. It runs the CLI against a mock Ollama server and asserts that the delivered prompt contains "Bring your expert judgment", the requirement text, definition text, the cited code (`fn ready()`) and test (`fn ready_test()`), and "submit_judgment exactly once". It also asserts that the tool set is correct and that a FIXME outcome is recorded with its evidence.
- `false_is_a_completed_assessment` (about lines 415–450) asserts that the prompt contains "Choose false for other gaps or insufficient evidence". It also asserts that the prompt contains the source comment `FIXME(#125): zero-capacity insertion panics` and the offending code. That covers the false outcome and the acknowledged-gap convention.
- The Bedrock test (~line 707) checks that the same prompt reaches the other provider.
- The unit test in `src/authoring/mod.rs` (~line 577) checks the opening of the Rust-function variant of the prompt.

**Judgment.** The logic is a simple template extraction and substitution. The tests cover prompt delivery on both providers, the true/FIXME and false outcomes, and the delivery of cited code and tests. Individual guidance sentences, such as the example-specific wording, are not asserted one by one. Because the prompt is taken verbatim from the approved template, that is a minor gap, not a missing obligation. I found no FIXME markers relevant to this subject, and I judge the requirement satisfied.

Source files and book chapters can mark lines as implementing, citing, or testing a requirement or example:
Each reference must name an existing requirement or example. Its evidence must include an input covering the line with the reference. In the book, references and definitions become linked badges.

For Rust, Habeas parses first-party source files and requires every explicit function or method, including trait methods and test helpers, to have a requirement or named example reference in an attached comment or its body. Each named example cites a requirement. A reference on an enclosing `impl` or module, in a string literal, or only in an evidence input does not cover the function. A Rust source file that cannot be parsed is reported as an error. For a helper with no behavior-specific requirement, agree on an explicit project requirement such as `internal-detail` and provide evidence explaining why it adds no otherwise unspecified user-visible behavior.

Rust-item selectors use syntactic ancestry within one repository-relative file. Examples include `mod[local]/fn[run]`, `impl[Thing]/fn[run]`, `impl[Thing/Trait]/fn[run]`, `trait[Trait]/fn[read]`, `fn[outer]/fn[inner]`, and positional `use#1`. Duplicate sibling names gain `#1`, `#2`, and so on. Delimiter characters and whitespace within names or impl types use percent-encoded UTF-8 bytes, so spelling can be recovered without resolving modules across files. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_selectors`

Each Rust function also needs an attestation in `evidence/rust/<rust_file>.json`, with a `rust_file` field and a `functions` array. Every entry has `rust_item`, a `citations` array of `{ "role": "impl", "name": "requirements.some_name" }` objects, a boolean `determination`, `rationale`, and `inputs`. This determination assesses citation coverage; FIXME applies to requirement and example judgments. It needs one Rust-item input for that function and at least one requirements input covering every cited definition. The agent must review the whole function and relevant definitions, then explain why its citations include *every applicable* requirement or named example and how those texts account for its behavior together. A matching snapshot alone is insufficient. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_function_attestations` {cite}`requirements.cli.function_attestation_guidance`

For Rust, Habeas parses first-party source files and requires every explicit function or method, including trait methods and test helpers, to have a requirement or named example reference in an attached comment or its body. Each named example cites a requirement. A reference on an enclosing `impl` or module, in a string literal, or only in an evidence input does not cover the function. A Rust source file that cannot be parsed is reported as an error. For a helper with no behavior-specific requirement, agree on an explicit project requirement such as `internal-detail` and provide evidence explaining why it adds no otherwise unspecified user-visible behavior.

Rust-item selectors use syntactic ancestry within one repository-relative file. Examples include `mod[local]/fn[run]`, `impl[Thing]/fn[run]`, `impl[Thing/Trait]/fn[run]`, `trait[Trait]/fn[read]`, `fn[outer]/fn[inner]`, and positional `use#1`. Duplicate sibling names gain `#1`, `#2`, and so on. Delimiter characters and whitespace within names or impl types use percent-encoded UTF-8 bytes, so spelling can be recovered without resolving modules across files. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_selectors`

Each Rust function also needs an attestation in `evidence/rust/<rust_file>.json`, with a `rust_file` field and a `functions` array. Every entry has `rust_item`, a `citations` array of `{ "role": "impl", "name": "requirements.some_name" }` objects, a boolean `determination`, `rationale`, and `inputs`. This determination assesses citation coverage; FIXME applies to requirement and example judgments. It needs one Rust-item input for that function and at least one requirements input covering every cited definition. The agent must review the whole function and relevant definitions, then explain why its citations include *every applicable* requirement or named example and how those texts account for its behavior together.
